title: Cap. 6 Arg. 3 Obj. 1–2: Preacher neglect and ancestral contempt do not bind God
pass_a_gloss: But some meet this argument by answering that the reason the Gospel is not preached everywhere is not so much that God does not send those who would preach, as that those who are sent refuse to go. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 105. But if God, by reason of his goodness and justice, as if from a certain congruence, Christ’s death being supposed, were bound to communicate sufficient means of application to all, he would not allow anyone to be cheated of an owed benefit by another’s carelessness—especially such a benefit, without which no salvation is to be hoped for. Indeed it implies a contradiction that God by ordinary law should provide and administer to all these means that look to the application of Christ, and yet not administer the same to some because of the preachers’ carelessness—when the very care of the preachers would have to be counted among those means, without which knowledge and application of the Christ preached cannot be had. Further, if God’s goodness or justice required that these means of applying Christ be administered to all, he would without doubt have kindled in at least some preachers this mind and this care of preaching and carrying the Gospel forward to every nation. For he himself is the one who knows how to thrust laborers into the harvest according to his good pleasure. Finally, what carelessness of preachers was the cause that two hundred years ago the Gospel was preached by no one to the Americans, when no one had even dreamed of these nations? One must therefore return to a higher cause, namely God’s free good pleasure in granting or denying these means, who by a certain special providence procures them to be administered to peoples, or not administered, through his ministers, as may be seen in Acts 16:6 and following: “They were forbidden to speak the word of God in Asia, and they were intending to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them,” and so on. Second, they answer that those who for a long time lacked evangelical grace had repudiated it in their ancestors: and so the descendants are deservedly deprived of the proclamation of the Gospel which their ancestors despised. Therefore it is not to be referred to God’s absolute will that some are not illuminated by the saving light of the Gospel. But neither do these things hang well with those people’s opinions. For if God, with respect had to Christ’s death, is bound to administer sufficient means of salvation to all humans, it seems little fair that, because of the preaching of the word despised by the ancestors in Noah’s times, the Gospel should be denied to their posterity after many thousands of years. For if, Adam’s sin notwithstanding, it has been obtained by Christ’s death (on their view) that sufficient means of salvation be administered to all, it is alien to reason and equity to break this quasi-ordinary law on the pretext of sins committed by any other ancestors of ours. So just as on account of Adam’s sin itself God could justly deny any spiritual benefit to his posterity, so we confess that from the sins of other ancestors God can also take occasion to deny us any free benefit. But if by Christ’s death, God’s goodness concurring, a law has been established about administering the means of grace, then just as on account of Adam’s sin—who bore in himself the person of all his posterity—God does not will to abrogate this his quasi-statute, so on account of the sins of others, who by no means sustain this common person of the human race, it is much less fitting that posterity be deprived of this benefit. In vain therefore they flee to the sins of the ancestors to give a reason for that denied thing which, by the virtue of Christ’s death and of divine goodness, they profess to have been prepared for all and each by divine decree and as if owed by a fixed law.
pass_b_english: Some meet this argument by saying the gospel is not preached everywhere less because God fails to send preachers than because those who are sent refuse to go. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 105. But if God, by his goodness and justice, as if by a kind of congruence, and with Christ’s death supposed, were bound to communicate sufficient means of application to everyone, he would not let anyone be cheated of an owed benefit by another’s carelessness—least of all a benefit without which no salvation can be hoped for. It is even a contradiction to say that by ordinary law God provides and administers to all these means that look to applying Christ, and yet withholds them from some because of the preachers’ neglect—when the very care of the preachers would have to be counted among those means, without which knowledge and application of the Christ who is preached cannot be had.

Further, if God’s goodness or justice required that these means of applying Christ be administered to all, he would without doubt have kindled in at least some preachers the will and care to preach and carry the gospel to every nation. He himself knows how to thrust laborers into the harvest according to his good pleasure. Finally, what preacher-neglect explains that two hundred years ago the gospel was preached by no one among the Americans, when no one had even dreamed those nations existed? We must therefore rise to a higher cause: God’s free good pleasure in granting or denying these means. By a special providence he sees to it that they are administered to peoples, or not administered, through his ministers—as Acts 16:6 and following shows: “They were forbidden to speak the word of God in Asia, and they were intending to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them,” and so on.

Second, they answer that those long without evangelical grace had already repudiated it in their ancestors, and so the descendants are rightly stripped of the gospel proclamation their ancestors despised; therefore the fact that some are not lit by the gospel’s saving light should not be referred to God’s absolute will. But this does not hang with their own views. If God, with an eye to Christ’s death, is bound to administer sufficient means of salvation to all people, it is hardly fair that, because ancestors despised the preached word in Noah’s day, the gospel should be denied to their posterity after many thousands of years. If—Adam’s sin notwithstanding—Christ’s death has (on their showing) secured that sufficient means of salvation be administered to all, it is alien to reason and equity to break that quasi-ordinary law on the pretext of sins committed by any other ancestors of ours.

Just as God could justly deny any spiritual benefit to Adam’s posterity because of Adam’s own sin, so we grant that from other ancestors’ sins God may also take occasion to deny us any free benefit. But if by Christ’s death, with God’s goodness concurring, a law has been set about administering the means of grace, then just as God will not abrogate that quasi-statute because of Adam’s sin—who bore in himself the person of all his posterity—so it is far less fitting that posterity be robbed of this benefit because of the sins of others who do not sustain that common person of the human race. They flee in vain to ancestral sins to explain the denial of a thing which, by the virtue of Christ’s death and of divine goodness, they themselves claim was prepared for all and each by divine decree and as if owed by fixed law.
source_text: Sed huic argumento occurrunt nonnulli respondendo, Quod Evangelium ubique non praedicetur, causa non tam haec est, quod a Deo non mittantur qui praedicent, quam quod qui mittuntur ire recusent. Sic Corvinus, contra Tilenum, pag. 105. Verum si Deus ratione bonitatis suae & justitiae, quasi ex congruitate quadam, Christi morte supposita, teneretur media applicationis sufficientia omnibus communicare, non sineret quenquam ob incuriam alterius debito beneficio fraudari, praesertim tali, absque quo nulla salus est sperabilis. Imo contradictionem implicat, Deum ex lege ordinaria providere & administrare omnibus haec media ad Christi applicationem spectantia, & quibusdam eadem non administrare, obstante scilicet praedicatorum incuria: Cum ipsa cura praedicatorum non esset annumeranda hisce mediis, sine quibus cognitio & applicatio Christi praedicati haberi nequit. Porro, Si Dei bonitas aut justitia hoc requireret, ut haec media Christi applicandi omnibus administrarentur, proculdubio in aliquibus saltem praedicatoribus hunc animum & hanc curam praedicandi & proferendi Evangelii ad singulas nationes accendisset. Ipse enim est qui operarios pro beneplacito suo novit in messem protrudere. Denique quae incuria praedicatorum in causa fuit, quod ducentis ab hinc annis Evangelium Americanis a nemine fuit praedicatum, quando de hisce nationibus nemo per somnium cogitaverat? Redeundum itaque est ad causam altiorem, nempe liberum Dei beneplacitum in hisce mediis gratificandis, aut negandis, qui per specialem quandam providentiam ea procurat administranda populis, vel non administranda per ministros suos, ut videre licet Actor. xvi. 6 &c. Vetiti sunt loqui verbum Dei in Asia, & tendebant ire in Bithyniam, & non permisit Spiritus, &c. Secundo respondent, eos qui longo tempore gratia Evangelica caruerunt, eam a majoribus suis repudiavisse: & sic posteros merito privari praeconio Evangelii, quod majores illorum contempserunt: Non itaque ad absolutam Dei voluntatem referendum esse, quod quidam salutari luce Evangelii non illustrentur. Sed neque haec bene cohaerent cum istorum placitis. Nam si Deus, ad mortem Christi habito respectu, omnibus hominibus tenetur media salutis sufficienter administrare, parum aequum videtur ut, propter praedicationem verbi temporibus Noachi a majoribus contemptam, Evangelium post multa annorum millia eorundem posteris denegatur. Si enim, non obstante Adami peccato, Christi morte impetratum sit (ex istorum sententia) ut media salutis sufficientia omnibus administrentur, a ratione & aequitate alienum est, hanc legem quasi ordinariam infringere, praetextu peccatorum ab aliis quibuscunque majoribus nostris commissorum. Sicut igitur propter ipsum Adami peccatum Deus juste possit posteris ejus quodvis beneficium spirituale denegare, ita fatemur, ex peccatis aliorum majorum posse quoque Deum occasionem sumere negandi nobis quodvis beneficium gratuitum. Verum si Christi morte, Dei bonitate concurrente, lex stabilita sit de administrandis gratiae mediis; jam sicut propter Adami peccatum, qui gessit in se personam omnium suorum posterorum, Deus non vult hoc suum quasi statutum abrogare, ita propter peccata aliorum, qui minime sustinent hanc communem humani generis personam, multo minus consentaneum est ut posteri hoc beneficio priventur. Frustra igitur ad peccata majorum confugiunt, ut ejus rei negatae rationem reddant, quam virtute mortis Christi ac bonitatis Divinae omnibus & singulis, ex decreto Divino praeparatam atque statuta lege quasi debitam, praefitentur.
